tag_list: Common Merganser (Mergus merganser) – female, River Place Marina, Portland, Oregon, waterfowl, mergansers, fall, All About Birds, Cornell University Lab of Ornithology, Northwest Birding, range, North America, United States, Canada, Mexico, Pacific Northwest, Western Hemisphere
description:
Common Merganser (Mergus merganser) – female 

23 October 2015: Walked down to the River Place Marina and the South Waterfront Park Garden next to the Willamette River a few miles before it joins the mighty Columbia River where the cities of Portland, Oregon and Vancouver, Washington, were founded and meet on opposite sides of the Columbia. It was early in the morning and we were able to photograph the sunrise over the Willamette and Portland while on our hike to the banks of the river. There were many homeless people on the waterfront with pitched tents on the sandbars of the river as well and sleeping on the park benches. There was also what must be the usual large contingent of early morning risers who do their running, jogging and bicycling before, during and right after sunrise. It was a morning and place of stark contrasts. The sunlight was a bit hazy as the night’s humidity lifted slowly as the morning progressed. One of the first birds we photographed were several female Common Mergansers (Mergus merganser) who kept their distance from us as zones of proximity go when working with wildlife. And so these were the best pics we managed on this particular day. Common Merganser was diving for food at sunrise on the Willamette River. We had never photographed Common Merganser before and the male of the species was nowhere to be seen. In order to highlight the basic features of Common Merganser we have Lightroomed the pics in order to bring out the light as these pics were taken with the predawn light just before the sun lifted its face above the eastern horizon of the city and the river. 

According to the range map on All About Birds, Common Merganser is a year-round resident of most of the Pacific Northwest (see Sources). Common Merganser is found throughout North America and most of the continental United States except for most of Texas and the rest of the Southeast and South of the nation. The farthest southeastern reach of this species is extreme West Texas including El Paso and the Big Bend area taking up parts of northern Mexico in Coahuila, Chihuahua and Sonora. Most of Canada and Alaska know the presence of Common Merganser either as a breeding or migratory species and Common Merganser’s permanent and breeding range extends into the Alaskan coastline as far as the Aleutian Islands. Because of its extensive presence over the North American map especially that of United States, Canada and Mexico, Common Merganser is without question an authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere.

Here is the brief description of this North American waterfowl provided in All About Birds: “Common Mergansers are streamlined ducks that float gracefully down small rivers or shallow shorelines. The males are striking with clean white bodies, dark green heads, and a slender, serrated red bill. The elegant gray-bodied females have rich, cinnamon heads with a short crest. In summer, look for them leading ducklings from eddy to eddy along streams or standing on a flat rock in the middle of the current. These large ducks nest in hollow trees; in winter they form flocks on larger bodies of water.”

Sources: 

“Common Merganser,” All About Birds, Cornell University Lab of Ornithology, range map, description, recorded calls, photogrpahs, accessed 10.30.15, http://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Common_Merganser/id

“Common Merganser,” Northwest Birding, photographs, and brief description, accessed 10.30.15, http://northwestbirding.com/Birds/common_merganser.html

When I first looked at this picture in detail, I thought I might have  two different species of merganser swimming together. The one in the rear appears to have a much sharper demarcation between the brown head and white chest (features found on a female Common Merganser) while the one in the lead has a tawny-brownish head and neck that appears to grade into a grayish  throat and breast, features consistent with a female Red-breasted Merganser. The bill on the one in the back appears wider at its base than the one in front's, as would be expected in a Common, but it has a clearly steep forehead, a feature more likely on a Red-breasted.  

After referring to several sources, I believe these are both Red-breasted Mergansers. The one in the back may be a first spring male who starting to show some darkening in the head and neck, increasing the contrast with the throat. The clincher was the feathering on the bill. The feathers on both birds extend on to the upper mandible. On a Common Merganser, the feathering comes down as a vertical border on the rear margin of the upper mandible.

description: At Union City Dam. In the outflow

Today I got an opportunity to see a species of waterfowl I have never seen before. The Red-breasted Merganser is an interesting bird to observe. The physical appearance alone is enough to catch the eye. Although the pictures are not entirely definitive because of the range they were taken, but the tell tale sign of the spiked up feathers on the hind side of the head are noticable. I observed only two mergansers together, but they stayed close with eachother. There was one other smaller water-fowl I noticed but it soon left the two. I witnessed the birds dive in the water a few times, and lift their chests while swimming. These two birds have beautiful colors to their body. Their chest being very white in color which makes me beielive they were females. Red-breasted Mergansers are about 23 inches in length. They have a black back, rusty chest, grey sides, a ring of white on the neck, and a dark green head. The bill is long, slender, and reddish in color. These birds usually are in groups of 6-12, this observation being an exception since there was only two. They prefer inshore oceans, coastal waters, and lakes. Overall, I'm happy to have the chance to experience this species especially since it's a one I've never seen.

description:
@gpstewart and I are on a week-long birding/nature/photography trip to west Texas and adjacent New Mexico. After a couple of days in the Texas Panhandle we made it into the small town of Clayton in far n.e. New Mexico. Weather predictions for the night of Dec. 12 and all day Dec. 13 were for a strong cold front with sustained 35-40 mph winds with gusts to 60 mph, described as dangerous highway conditions with some high profile vehicles like tractor trailers that might blow over. We decided to stay all day the 13th in Clayton and stay off the highways till the weather calmed down a little. Sure enough, this morning (Dec. 13) winds were strong enough to make walking difficult and at 26 degrees and 40 mph winds it was interesting to say the least. Regardless of the weather, we decided to spend a few hours on small dirt roads north of Clayton out into the prairies to see what we could find as sitting in a motel all day was not too appealing to either of us. As expected, weather and blowing sand, blowing tumbleweeds, blowing small pebbles etc., made it interesting. Visited Clayton Lake State Park and had a few distant birds on the water such as 5 Common Mergansers, 3 Canada Geese etc., in protected coves but due to distance, etc., images will be marginal at best. At one point I tried to stand outside of the truck to take some shots and I almost had my camera ripped from my hands by the wind. So, anyway, today a day of marginal quality shots and tough weather. Hope to improve on both tomorrow. All days in nature are interesting, however!

Common mergansers are skilled diving predators, eating mainly slower small fish. Their serrated bills are well suited for capturing small fish and other aquatic prey.

description:
White Rock lake, near banks of sunset bay beach

Perfect Pose
My 2nd encounter with this rare visitor came a half hour later in a different part of the lake.  I had finished exploring other areas and was returning to my car when I spotted her right by the shore at Sunset Bay beach.  Just chilling and hanging out.  She was no longer shy and let me get several nice shots of her.  There was  no one else around at the time & I could not believe my luck.  She has such a long body compared to hooded mergansers.
Photo 2:
Bizarre Merganser Face Shot
I thought she was beautiful right up until she looked straight at me.  Uggg, your profile is much better my dear.  Who knew she had a mug like that.  No worries, after a moment of adjustment, I went back to noticing her nicer features.   I love that she is a ginger.
Photo 3:
Gingers Have More Fun
Last shot from my first encounter with a common merganser.  This light showed off those pretty red head feathers as she swam off into the sun with a coot.

Week 3 of this rare duck visiting White Rock lake.  This was my 3rd week to see her.  I was sitting on the pier when she showed up and slowly swam back and forth in front of the pier.  I'm not sure if she was looking for a handout but she kept a safe distance.  I took advantage & got shots of her from both directions.  The sun cooperated and lit her up for me.  I was practically holding my breath so I would not scare her off.  She is so pretty.  She swam further out and away, was only close for a couple of minutes.  I got one nice close up face shot before she moved further out.  Very cool that you can see the serrated edges of her bill on top and bottom in the gap.  Hence the term saw-toothed bill ducks.

The first photo shows two male Red-breasted Merganser(Mergus Serrator). I observed numerous pairs of Red-breasted Mergansers  in courtship display(see second photo). 

"In courtship display, male stretches neck forward and upward, then suddenly dips neck and forepart of body underwater, with head angled up out of water and bill open wide. Nest: female selects site on ground, usually near water, in a spot sheltered by dense plant growth or debris. Sometimes nests inside hollow stump, under rock, or in shallow burrow. Nest is a simple depression, lined with down.

This sea-going duck is notable for its long, red, serrated bill, which gives it the species name serrator. It is a diver — as referenced in its genus name Mergus, or diver — able to stay beneath the water’s surface for almost a minute while foraging as deep as 15 to 20 feet.

One of the Red-breasted Merganser’s notable features is a shaggy-looking double crest The colorful male sports a metallic-green head, white neck band and wing patches, a red bill and eyes, and a reddish, black-speckled breast, for which the bird is named. The female is mostly gray with an orange-brown head."(Audubon)
